slides.say: k, a, b and c are integers. Given: two k plus one is equal to a cubed, times b plus one, squared, times c minus five, to the power of four. Which of the numbers k, a, b, c is necessarily odd?
It looks complicated, but we only need the rule for an odd product. [short pause] We'll solve it two ways, using that rule, and then plugging in numbers.

[short pause] Let's start with the left side, two k plus one. Two times any integer is even, and adding one makes it odd. If k is two, we get five. If k is three, we get seven. So the left side is odd, whether k is even or odd.

The right side equals the left, so it must be odd too. A product is odd only when every number we multiply is odd. One even number would make the whole product even. The powers keep each number even or odd, so let's check the numbers inside those powers.
a cubed is odd, so a must be odd. b plus one must be odd, so b must be even. c minus five must be odd, so c must be even. Only a must be odd. Choice number two is our answer.
at: choice number two is our answer

slides.say: [pause] Now let's try plugging in. To rule out the other choices, look for a case where k, b and c are even. Use a is one, b is zero, and c is six. One cubed is one, zero plus one is one, and six minus five is one. Raising those ones to their powers keeps them one. So the whole right side is one.
at: a is one, b is zero

slides.say: Then two k plus one is one, so k is zero. k, b and c are all even in this example, and the equation works. So choice numbers one, three and four are out. Choice number two is our answer. Okay. I'll see you in the next question.
at: Two k plus one is one
